info.name: Cookiepot API — v1
info.description:
Cookiepot backend API.

## Getting started

1. Start MongoDB and the server:
   ```bash
   mongod --dbpath ~/data/mongodb --logpath ~/data/mongolog/mongod.log --fork
   cd backend && pnpm install && pnpm seed && pnpm dev
   ```
2. Pick the **Cookiepot — Local** environment (or keep the collection defaults).
3. Run **Auth → Login (super_admin)**. Tokens are captured into collection variables automatically by a test script, so every authenticated request below just works.

## Seed accounts

All use password `Pass123!word`.

| Email | Role | Status |
|---|---|---|
| root@test.test | super_admin | active |
| admin@test.test | admin | active |
| mod@test.test | moderator | active |
| active@test.test | user | active |
| pending@test.test | user | pending |
| suspended@test.test | user | suspended |
| banned@test.test | user | banned |

## Response envelope

Success: `{ "data": T, "meta"?: { next_cursor, has_more } }`

Error:
```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "account_suspended",
    "message": "Your account is suspended, so that action is unavailable.",
    "severity": 40,
    "field_errors": { "email": ["Enter a valid email address"] },
    "rejection_reason": "status_suspended_blocked"
  }
}
```

- **`code`** — branch on this and only this. It is the contract.
- **`message`** — display verbatim. Free to change, so never branch on it.
- **`severity`** — dashboards only. Clients ignore it.
- **`field_errors`** — validation failures only; **all** invalid fields, not just the first.
- **`rejection_reason`** — operator diagnostic. **Not contract** — never branch on it.

Severity bands: 10 body-validation · 20 suspicious-validation · 30 auth · 40 forbidden · 50 not-found · 60 conflict · 70 business-rule · 80 rate-limited · 90 upstream · 100 server-fault.

## Permissions — two independent axes

Role and status gate separately, deliberately: a suspended admin is still an admin and must still be refused.

| Status | Holds a session | Reads own profile | Writes |
|---|---|---|---|
| pending | yes | yes | no — `account_pending_verification` |
| active | yes | yes | yes |
| suspended | yes | yes | no — `account_suspended` |
| banned | no — refused at login | — | — |
| deleted | no — refused at login | — | — |

## Rate limiting

Token bucket. Every response carries `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset`; a 429 also carries a real `Retry-After` in seconds. Login is limited by IP **and** by email. Storage is in-memory and per-process, so restarting the server resets every bucket.

item.name: Health
item.description: Infrastructure probes. Deliberately unversioned — they are not API surface and must not move when the API version does.

request.description:
Is the process up?

Checks nothing external on purpose. A liveness probe that fails when the database is down gets the container killed and restarted — which does not fix a database, and does drop in-flight requests.

**200** `{ data: { status, message, uptime_seconds, database } }`

response.name: 200 OK

request.description:
Should this instance receive traffic?

This one **does** ping the database: an instance that cannot reach it can serve nothing useful and should be pulled from the load balancer.

**200** ready · **503** `upstream_failure` with `Retry-After: 5`

response.name: 200 Ready
503 Database unreachable

item.name: Auth
item.description:
Registration, sessions, and password change.

Access JWT (15 min) plus an opaque refresh token (30 days) that is **rotated on every use** — a refresh token is good exactly once. Replaying one that was already rotated means two parties hold it, so every session for that user is revoked.

Refresh tokens are stored hashed (SHA-256): a database dump yields no usable sessions.

exec: pm.test('new accounts start pending, not active', function () {
pm.test('email is normalised to lowercase', function () {
pm.test('password is never echoed back', function () {

request.description:
Create an account and open a session.

The new account is **`pending`**, not active — it can read its own profile but cannot write until an admin activates it (email verification is not built yet; see the QA handoff).

**Password policy:** min 8 chars, at least one lowercase, one uppercase, one digit.

**Rate limit:** 5/hour per IP — registration is cheap to abuse and expensive to serve (argon2 + an email).

**201** session · **409** `email_exists` · **422** `validation_error` · **429** `rate_limited`

The email is lowercased and trimmed at the boundary so the unique index is genuinely case-insensitive.

response.name: 201 Created
409 Email already exists
422 Validation error

request.description:
**Run this first.** Captures the tokens into collection variables, so every authenticated request below works without copy-pasting.

Email matching is case-insensitive.

**Rate limit:** 10 per 15 min per IP **and** 10 per 15 min per email. The two are separate buckets — IP rotation alone should not buy unlimited guesses against one account.

**Account lockout:** 5 consecutive failures locks the account for 15 minutes, and the correct password is refused during the lock (`account_locked`, 429, with `Retry-After`). That counter lives on the user record, not the limiter, so it survives a restart.

An unknown email and a wrong password return the **same** `invalid_credentials` — distinguishing them turns the endpoint into an account-existence oracle. A `banned` or `deleted` account is refused outright.

**200** session · **401** `invalid_credentials` · **403** `account_banned` · **429** `account_locked` / `rate_limited`

response.name: 200 OK
401 Invalid credentials
403 Account banned
429 Account locked
429 Rate limited

request.description: Sign in as `admin`. Can list and read users, and change statuses — but **cannot** change roles (super_admin only). Use this to see the role gate refuse a role change.
Sign in as a plain `active` user. Use this to watch the **role** gate refuse the admin endpoints with `insufficient_role`.

exec: pm.test('a suspended account may still hold a session', function () {

request.description:
A `suspended` account **can** sign in and read its own profile, but every write is refused with `account_suspended`.

Use this to watch the **status** gate — the axis a role check cannot cover. Sign in here, then run *Users → Update my profile* and see the 403.

exec: pm.test('refresh token is rotated — the old one is now dead', function () {

request.description:
Exchange a refresh token for a new pair. The presented token is revoked in the same step — **a refresh token is good exactly once.**

**Reuse detection.** Presenting a token that was already rotated away means two parties hold it, and there is no way to tell which one is asking. Every session for that user is revoked and the response is `session_revoked`. Run this request twice in a row to see it.

A logout or password change revokes with a *reason*, so an ordinary sign-out reports `token_invalid` and is **not** treated as theft — otherwise signing out on one device would sign you out everywhere.

Refresh is also where a mid-session ban takes effect: access-token claims are stale by design, and this is where they are re-checked against the database.

| What happened | `code` |
|---|---|
| rotated, then replayed | `session_revoked` |
| sibling session killed by that incident | `session_revoked` |
| logged out normally | `token_invalid` |
| password changed | `token_invalid` |
| banned mid-session | `account_banned` |

**Rate limit:** 60 per 15 min per IP.

**200** new session · **401** `token_invalid` / `token_expired` / `session_revoked` · **403** `account_banned`

response.name: 200 Rotated
401 Reuse detected — all sessions revoked
401 Token invalid (after logout)

exec: pm.test('logout returns 204 with no body', function () {

request.description:
End the session that owns this refresh token.

Takes the refresh token in the body rather than requiring a valid access token — a client whose access token has already expired must still be able to sign out.

**Idempotent.** An unknown or already-revoked token still means "you are signed out", so it returns 204 either way. Reporting an error here only confuses a client that is retrying.

**204** — no body at all. Do not call `.json()` on this response.

Only this session is revoked; other devices stay signed in. That is the whole reason logout carries a distinct revocation reason internally.

Change the signed-in user's password.

**Every session is revoked**, including the one making this call — that is the point of changing a password after a suspected compromise. Sign in again afterwards.

A confirmation email is sent (logged rather than sent when `RESEND_API_KEY` is empty).

**Status gate:** `active` **or** `pending`. An unverified user must not be locked out of their own credentials.

**Rate limit:** 5/hour per user.

**204** changed · **401** `invalid_credentials` (wrong current password) · **422** `validation_error` (new password fails policy)

⚠️ Running this invalidates the collection's captured tokens and changes the seed password for that account. Re-run `pnpm seed` to restore it.

response.name: 401 Wrong current password

item.name: Users — me
item.description:
The signed-in user's own profile.

These two endpoints are the clearest demonstration of the status gate: reading is open to `pending` and `suspended`, writing is `active` only.

**Route order is load-bearing.** `/users/me` is registered *before* `/users/:userId`, or Express matches the parameterised route first and "me" arrives as a literal user id — a 404 on the most-used endpoint in the app.

exec: pm.test('the password hash never crosses the wire', function () {

request.description:
The signed-in user's profile.

**Status gate:** `active`, `pending`, **or** `suspended` — a suspended user can still see their own account, which is how they learn why they cannot act.

**Rate limit:** 120/min.

**200** user · **401** `unauthenticated` / `token_invalid` / `token_expired`

The response comes from a single mapper, which is deliberately the only path from a document to a response — a field added to the model is never published by accident, and `passwordHash` cannot leak through it.

response.name: 200 OK
401 No token
401 Token expired

request.description:
Update the signed-in user's own profile. Only `name` is editable today.

**Status gate: `active` only.** This is the gate doing work a role check cannot — a suspended user keeps their role and still cannot change anything.

To see it fire, run *Auth → Login (suspended user)* and then this request: **403 `account_suspended`**. A freshly registered (`pending`) account gets **403 `account_pending_verification`**.

**Rate limit:** 30/min.

**200** updated user · **403** `account_suspended` / `account_pending_verification` · **422** `validation_error`

response.name: 200 Updated
403 Suspended — status gate blocks the write
403 Pending — email not verified

item.name: Users — administration
item.description:
Admin surface. Registered **after** `/users/me` so the literal path is not swallowed by `/users/:userId`.

Privilege is tiered deliberately:

| Action | Minimum role |
|---|---|
| list / read users | `admin` |
| change a status | `moderator` |
| change a **role** | `super_admin` |

Granting privilege is strictly super-admin: an admin who can mint admins is an admin who can escalate anyone, including a compromised account.

All of these also require the **caller** to be `active`.

query.description: 1–100. Defaults to 20. Clamped server-side — a client-sent limit is never trusted.
Opaque cursor from a previous response's meta.next_cursor. Never parse it. A malformed cursor falls back to the first page rather than erroring.
Filter: pending | active | suspended | banned | deleted

request.description:
List users, newest first.

**Cursor pagination only** — offset is banned. `skip(n)` re-scans n documents per page, and a concurrent insert shifts every later page, so a user scrolling a live list silently sees an item twice or misses it entirely.

The cursor encodes the last item's sort key **and** its id; the id breaks ties when two records share a timestamp, without which pagination stalls or skips.

Sets `{{target_user_id}}` from the first result, so the requests below work immediately.

**Role:** `admin` or above. **Rate limit:** 200/min.

**200** `{ data: User[], meta: { next_cursor, has_more } }` · **403** `insufficient_role`

response.name: 200 OK
403 Insufficient role

request.description:
Follow the cursor from the previous request. Run *List users* first to populate `{{next_cursor}}`.

Pages are disjoint — no id appears on two pages, which is exactly the property offset pagination loses under concurrent inserts.

variable.description: Prefixed ULID, e.g. u_01m101enr9xk32bjzd16arp3zg. Opaque — never parse it.

request.description:
Fetch one user.

Ids are resource-prefixed ULIDs (`u_…`): self-describing in a log line, and monotonically sortable, which is what lets them serve as a pagination tiebreak. Clients treat them as opaque strings.

**Role:** `admin` or above. **Rate limit:** 200/min.

**200** user · **403** `insufficient_role` · **404** `not_found`

response.name: 404 Not found

request.description:
Move a user between lifecycle statuses. `status` is one of `pending | active | suspended | banned | deleted`; `reason` is optional and shown in admin tooling.

**The transition must be legal.** The application owns the transition map — the schema only constrains the *value*, not the *move* — and a client-sent status is untrusted until checked against it:

| From | May go to |
|---|---|
| pending | active, banned, deleted |
| active | suspended, banned, deleted |
| suspended | active, banned, deleted |
| banned | active, deleted |
| deleted | — (terminal) |

**Moving a user out of a session-eligible status revokes their sessions immediately** — otherwise a banned user keeps acting until their access token expires. A notification email is sent.

Setting the status to its current value is a no-op that returns 200.

**Role:** `moderator` or above. **Rate limit:** 200/min.

**200** updated · **403** `insufficient_role` · **404** `not_found` · **422** `validation_error` (illegal transition)

response.name: 200 Updated
422 Illegal transition

request.description:
Change a user's role. One of `user | moderator | admin | super_admin`.

**Super admin only.** An admin who can mint admins is an admin who can escalate anyone, including a compromised account. Sign in as `admin@test.test` and run this to see **403 `insufficient_role`** with `rejection_reason: role_below_super_admin`.

**You cannot change your own role.** Self-demotion is how an organisation locks itself out of its own admin tooling; another super admin must do it. Returns **403 `forbidden`** with the message "You cannot change your own role."

The target's sessions are revoked so their next sign-in mints a token with the correct claims — the old access token still carries the old role until it expires.

**Rate limit:** 200/min.

**200** updated · **403** `insufficient_role` / `forbidden` (self) · **404** `not_found` · **422** `validation_error`

response.name: 200 Updated
403 Not super_admin
403 Cannot change own role

item.name: Error envelope — worked examples
item.description:
Requests that deliberately fail, so the envelope can be inspected without hunting for a way to break something.

Run these to see the four error shapes a client must handle.

request.description:
An unparseable body is a **client** error, not a server one.

Express's body parser throws a `SyntaxError`; left to fall through it renders as a 500 and inflates the error-rate alarm for what is squarely a client mistake. It is caught explicitly and returned as **400 `malformed_json`**.

response.name: 400 Malformed JSON

request.description:
An unmatched path returns the standard envelope, not Express's HTML error page.

Note it is a **404**, not a 401 — `authenticate` is attached per route rather than via `router.use()`, which would run for unmatched paths too and tell an anonymous caller to "sign in" about a route that does not exist.

response.name: 404 Not found

request.description:
A garbage bearer token returns **`token_invalid`**.

An *expired* one returns **`token_expired`** instead — the client needs to tell them apart, because one is resolved by refreshing and the other by signing in again.

response.name: 401 Token invalid

request.description:
**Policy: all invalid fields are returned, not just the first.**

That is a product decision, and it is applied identically in the validation middleware and the error handler — splitting it between the two is how a form shows one error on submit and five on re-render.

Unknown keys are stripped by the schema, so a client cannot smuggle an extra field through to a service.

response.name: 422 Validation error
